The Hebrew Bible. The Hebrew Bible, also known as the Tanakh, an acronym for its three divisions—Torah, Nevi'im, and Ketuvim—is the sacred scripture of Judaism and the basis of the Christian Old Testament. Composed over nearly a thousand years and written in Hebrew and Aramaic, it contains narratives of creation, covenant, law, prophecy, and wisdom that form the foundation of monotheistic religion and Western ethical thought.

The Torah, also called the Five Books of Moses, comprises Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. They form the foundational narrative and legal code of Judaism. The Nevi'im, or Prophets, include the Former Prophets—Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings—and the Latter Prophets—Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Twelve Minor Prophets. The Ketuvim, or Writings, encompass the Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah, and Chronicles.

Key narratives include the creation of humanity, the Flood, the covenant with Abraham, the Exodus from Egypt under Moses, and the kingdom of David. Major themes include covenant and election, divine justice, prophecy as God's communication with humanity, and wisdom as moral insight. Christians adopted the Hebrew Bible as the Old Testament, reading it as prophetic of Jesus and the New Covenant, which fundamentally shaped Christian hermeneutics and theology.
